sections.html:
Richmond, the state capital, answers to no county. It gained independent-city status in 1871 after incorporating in 1742. The 2025 estimate is 237,257 residents, up from 226,610 in the 2020 census, which makes Richmond the fourth most populous city in the state.

People here describe the city in four parts: the North Side, Southside, East End and West End. Housing runs from Victorian townhouses to mid-century ranches, so the story of a house depends a lot on which side of the James River it stands.

Part of townNeighborhoods
East EndChurch Hill (home to St. John's Church), Fulton, Union Hill, Fairmount
The Fan and Museum DistrictMonument Avenue and many Victorian buildings, beside the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts

sections.h2: How Richmond grew, and why it matters for older houses
sections.html:
The first street grid dates to 1737 and covered the land between today's Broad, 17th and 25th streets and the river. Downtown now sits a little west of that, on the slopes of Shockoe Hill. Many North Side districts were built up after the streetcar arrived and are now listed historic districts.

Southside has its own story. Richmond absorbed the former city of Manchester in 1910. On January 1, 1970, the city grew south by 27 square miles and picked up 47,000 residents, after Chesterfield County lost a court fight against the annexation. Houses on opposite sides of the river can differ in age, lot size and repair needs even when they sit only a mile or two apart.

The James River reaches tidewater at Richmond, and flooding can happen in any month, most often in March and least often in July. Hurricanes and tropical storms have caused most summer and early fall floods. Three hurricanes in 1955, Connie and Diane among them, brought record rainfall over six weeks. In 2004 the remnants of Hurricane Gaston dropped up to 12 inches of rain and did extensive damage downtown.

A flood wall finished in 1995 protects the low-lying parts of the city. Shockoe Bottom, the low ground between Shockoe Hill and Church Hill, is the area most tied to river flooding.

  • Find out whether your lot sits in a mapped floodplain before you list.
  • Check the basement or lowest floor for stains, mold or a sump pump that no longer runs.
  • Pull together insurance and repair records for past water damage.

Winters are moderately cold and summers hot and humid. Snow averages 10.5 inches a season, though it rarely lingers more than a day or two, and ice storms are common but seldom severe. The real risk is an empty house during a cold snap. In an unheated house, one leaky pipe can become a big repair bill, and old roofs and gutters suffer as well.

With an inherited house you are not using, keep the heat on low or shut off the water, and ask someone to check in. Selling ends that worry.

Law, finance and government drive the economy. Downtown holds federal, state and local agencies plus large law and banking firms, and the metro area is home to several Fortune 500 companies. Virginia Commonwealth University and its Medical College of Virginia campus anchor the Virginia BioTechnology Research Park, which opened in 1995.

With that mix of employers, buyers come from many directions, and an owner of a damaged or dated house often weighs repair costs against selling as is. A cash buyer can give you a clear answer on the second option without pressure.

Both the Supreme Court of Virginia and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit sit here, so lawyers who handle probate, title and bankruptcy are easy to find. Selling for an estate? Ask the circuit court clerk what must be filed ahead of signing a deed, and keep the estate attorney informed.

Downtown has long been a hub for boats at the Great Turning Basin, for rail, and for two major interstates that cross. Interstates 95, 64 and 195 all touch the city's neighborhoods. The city is about 21 miles north of Petersburg and sits inside the larger Richmond-Petersburg metro area with Chesterfield, Henrico and Hanover counties.

When you describe your house, mention the nearest interstate access, which side of the river it is on and how far it is from VCU or downtown. Buyers weigh those details heavily.

Sale price triggers a state grantor tax of 50 cents per $500, owed by the seller unless the buyer agrees to take it on. No deed is recorded until the clerk certifies the tax, and the state and the locality divide it evenly. Read the law at Virginia Code 58.1-802.

Rates, due dates, assessment cycles and appeal deadlines change, so phone the city's real estate assessor and finance office before you pick a closing date. Any property tax still owed is deducted from your proceeds.

sections.h2: What to bring to a Richmond closing
sections.html: Pack a photo ID, your deed if you hold a copy, and mortgage account details if a loan remains. Landlords add the leases and tenant contacts, while heirs add proof of who can sign for the estate. On closing day the agent takes out the payoff, unpaid tax and recording fees and hands you the balance. An itemized estimate beforehand removes surprises.

sections.h2: Choosing between a listing and a direct sale
sections.html: Listing the usual way involves prep work, showings, repair talks after the inspection and a wait on the buyer's bank. Selling directly skips nearly all of it. Listing tends to suit a house in good shape when you can wait for the best price. A direct sale suits a house with damage, tenants, a probate calendar or a deadline. Whichever way you lean, compare what you would actually receive after taxes, repairs and holding costs, not just the headline number.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works for a Richmond house
sections.html:
A Richmond cash sale uses the same Virginia contract, title and deed steps as a financed one. The difference is that no lender is waiting on an appraisal, which shortens the timeline and removes a common reason deals fall apart.

  • Send us the address and a few details about condition and timing.
  • We review the house, and if an offer fits, it covers the property as it stands.
  • A settlement company searches the title and prepares the deed.
  • You choose a closing date, sign and collect your proceeds.

You do not clean out, repair or stage, and you can decline without owing anything. This route suits heirs, landlords and owners of worn houses anywhere from Southside to the East End who want a firm closing date.

faqs.q: What is the population of Richmond, VA?
faqs.a: The 2025 estimate is 237,257 residents, up from 226,610 in the 2020 census.

faqs.q: Does the James River flood in Richmond?
faqs.a: Yes. Flooding can occur in any month and is most common in March. A flood wall finished in 1995 protects the low-lying parts of the city.

faqs.q: When did Richmond grow south into Southside?
faqs.a: On January 1, 1970, the city annexed 27 square miles from Chesterfield County, adding about 47,000 residents.

faqs.q: Who pays the Virginia grantor tax in a Richmond sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it, at 50 cents per $500 of the price, unless the buyer agrees to cover some or all of it.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Richmond house that needs repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can purchase it as is, so you do not have to make repairs first.
